# Recap (II)

#### Course: Learn C Programming

## Recap (II)

### Type Conversion

You can convert one type of data to another; this is known as type conversion.

```c
1#include <stdio.h>
2
3int main() {
4    
5    float totalDistance = 89.5;
6    float distanceTravelled = 23.5;
7
8    float remainingDistance = totalDistance - distanceTravelled;
9
10    int approximateDistance = (int) remainingDistance;
11
12    printf("The approximate distance left is:  %d\n", approximateDistance);
13
14    return 0;
15}
```

### Taking User Input

You can take input from the user and use this value during program execution by using the scanf() function.

```c
1#include <stdio.h>
2
3int main() {
4
5    float distanceTravelled;
6
7    // Prompt the user to enter the travelled distance  
8    printf("Enter the distance you travelled: ");
9
10    // Take the user input
11    scanf("%f", &distanceTravelled);
12
13    printf("You travelled : %f kilometers so far", distanceTravelled);
14
15   return 0;
16}
```

With these foundational concepts in place, you can advance to the next lesson.

SRISATVIK

##### why should i keep int in brackets

Nisha Sharma from Programiz

Hello there,

When you write (int), you’re telling the compiler to force a value into an integer. C won’t just assume it’s okay to turn a float into an int, because that means dropping the decimal part. So the brackets act like a clear signal:

I know this is a float. I want it as an int. Do it exactly this way.

In your code:

```c
int approximateDistance = (int) remainingDistance;
```

You’re basically trimming off the decimal. Without the cast, the compiler will complain because it doesn’t want to guess your intention.

That’s all. It’s just you taking control instead of letting the compiler worry about it.
